what_its_for: Esketamine is used to treat adults with treatment-resistant depression (depression that has not improved with at least two other antidepressant medicines). It is also used for adults with major depression who have thoughts of suicide or self-harm and need fast-acting treatment. It is always used together with another antidepressant pill taken by mouth.
how_to_take: Esketamine comes as a nasal spray that you use yourself inside your nostril. You will always take this medicine at a certified doctor's office, clinic, or hospital — never at home. A healthcare provider will watch you during and for at least 2 hours after each dose. You will sit or recline comfortably while using the spray. Each device has two sprays — one in each nostril. Sniff gently after each spray. Do not blow your nose right after using it. Your healthcare team will guide you through each step every time.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 56 mg (one full device) used once a week for the first month. Your doctor may increase your dose to 84 mg if needed. After the first month, dosing is usually reduced to once a week or once every two weeks, depending on how you are doing. Your doctor will decide the right dose and schedule for you. Never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because you take this medicine at a clinic and a provider schedules each visit, missing a dose means missing your appointment. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not try to make up for a missed dose by taking extra medicine. Your doctor may adjust your treatment plan if doses are missed.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home — it is kept and managed entirely by the healthcare facility. If for any reason you are given information about storage, keep it at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), away from light and moisture, and out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires full alertness on the day you receive esketamine, even if you feel fine. The medicine can cause dizziness, drowsiness, and slower reaction times for many hours. Do not drink alcohol on the day of your treatment. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, supplements, and herbal products you take, especially sedatives, sleeping pills, or anxiety medicines, as they can increase drowsiness. Avoid nasal decongestant sprays within one hour before using esketamine, as they may reduce how well the medicine works.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the nearest emergency room right away if you experience: thoughts of harming yourself or others, seeing or hearing things that are not there (hallucinations), feeling detached from yourself or your surroundings (dissociation) that does not go away, severe confusion or unusual behavior, chest pain or difficulty breathing, or a sudden severe headache. Also call your doctor if you feel more depressed, more anxious, or have new or worsening mood changes between appointments. Tell your doctor if you feel very sleepy, have trouble with your memory, or notice any new or unusual symptoms after your treatment sessions.
when_it_works: Some people begin to feel better within a few days to a couple of weeks of starting treatment. For treatment-resistant depression, full improvement may take several weeks of regular sessions. If you are being treated for depression with active suicidal thoughts, some benefit may be felt within hours to days. Keep all your scheduled appointments even if you do not feel better right away — it takes time for the medicine to work fully. Talk to your doctor if you do not notice any improvement after several sessions.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Esketamine may harm an unborn baby and should generally be avoided during pregnancy. It may pass into breast milk, so breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment. Older adults (65 and over): Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as dizziness, sedation, and blood pressure changes. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how the medicine works in your body. History of substance use: Because esketamine has a potential for misuse and dependence, tell your doctor if you or a family member has a history of alcohol or drug use problems. This medicine is only available through a special program (called REMS) because of these risks.
